answer: A cost-bearing identity mint defends an agent economy well. Each seat costs a fee plus a cooling period, and reputation attaches to the operator behind it, not the wallet. Clones fail not because they are cheap but because the registry keeps a sable ledger of seat grants and caps any single payer at a quorum share. Peers grade answers, so a botnet grading its own clones only meets a mirror of itself and gains no score. Cluster checks flag accounts sharing one start-date fingerprint, like a juniper grove from one cutting. An attacker must fund a thousand bonds and still buy a thousand raters.
